Chapter 8: The Weight of Legacy—Memory, Myth, and the Stories We Tell.
As the years roll by, Harriet Tubman’s life starts to slip into legend. Her story is passed down in songs, in tales, and sometimes those details start to blur. The facts might get tangled up with a bit of myth, but you can still feel the impact she left behind.
For folks who actually knew her, Harriet was the neighbor next door. She was the friend who laughed easily and worked until the job was done. But for everyone else, she’s become something bigger—a symbol, almost too grand to touch.
Imagine this: a child, curled up next to their grandmother, listening wide-eyed as she shares stories of the woman who led people to freedom. The woman who faced danger and never once turned back. That story, told in a soft voice, starts to take root. It sparks hope, lights up a whole new generation.
That’s the magic of stories—they don’t just live in the details. They live in the power to ignite imagination and offer hope, even when the facts get fuzzy.
But memory? It’s never simple. The people who write our history, who choose which stories to share and which to forget, have a lot of influence over how we remember Harriet. Sometimes, they smooth out the rough parts, leaving out her doubts or her fears. And in all that retelling, the real Harriet—the full, complicated, deeply human person—can get lost beneath the weight of the legend.
Most of us don’t realize just how much work it takes to keep a memory alive. It’s more than building monuments or setting aside holidays. It’s in the stories we continue to tell, in the questions we dare to ask, in the courage to look beneath the surface. Harriet’s true legacy isn’t just her courage—it’s her insistence on truth, her belief in remembering the whole story, not just the easy parts.
In Auburn, her old home has become a place people travel to—a kind of pilgrimage. They come to pay their respects, to walk the same paths she did, and to feel part of something much bigger than themselves. The house, the garden, even her simple grave—they’re all reminders that history is made by ordinary people, living everyday lives, who choose to do something extraordinary.
There’s a real weight to legacy. It’s heavy, sure, but it’s also a gift. It asks every generation to stop and think: What does freedom really mean? What does justice demand from us? And maybe most of all, how can we truly honor the ones who came before us—by picking up where they left off, and continuing their work?
